title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation fraud in which AI-generated content was used to fabricate a fake interview between two named public figures, then deployed to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The failure is not one of a deployed AI product but of AI tools being used by bad actors outside any regulated deployment context. The content was polished enough to be plausible, and no institutional check existed at the point of distribution to flag that the interview never took place.

The scale reported by the regulator shows this is not an isolated case. Tens of thousands of similar scams were identified and removed in a single year, with deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians appearing with increasing frequency. The ease of producing convincing synthetic media has lowered the barrier for this kind of fraud, making volume and variety of attacks easier to sustain.

What is not established is who created the specific fake article, whether any individuals were charged, or whether Boulder Sparhaven was connected to any identified group. The regulator's figures describe scams removed, not convictions obtained, and a warning from a financial authority is not a legal finding against any named party.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article claiming Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock had a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler never actually occurred. The fabricated piece promoted Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform that Australian authorities warn against. This type of scam is becoming increasingly common as artificial intelligence makes deceptive content easier to create and more convincing to potential victims.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission research reveals that investment scams using deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians are rising sharply. Last year, the regulator removed 19,400 scams total, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and billionaire Gina Rinehart are among the most commonly impersonated Australians. ASIC urges consumers to verify financial services licenses through official registers and warns that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy.
